corrections.issue: The size of the supply disruption is not stated: the caption reads 'we lost a day of production' with no number, so '2 mb/d' is the first reader's guess (it is also not consistent with the Libya, Syria and Iran losses named). The speaker's point is that the disruptions and US shale growth were of similar size and cancelled out, with OPEC's spare capacity meeting about 1 mb/d of annual demand growth.
corrections.fix: Oil held near $110 for 3.5 years because Arab Spring and sanctions-related supply disruptions (Libya, Syria, Iraq, Iran, from 2010 to early 2014) were offset by a roughly equal rise in US shale output, while OPEC met demand growth of about 1 mb/d per year from spare capacity left after the financial crisis.

corrections.issue: 'Benefit from cheap crude' is not in the transcript: the speaker says US refiners are doing well, being the best refineries and operators with a Gulf Coast location, and that this has a shelf life of three to seven years, with some pain later but much less severe than Europe's.
corrections.fix: US refiners are doing very well now because they are among the best refineries and operators with a Gulf Coast location, but the advantage has a shelf life of three to seven years; some pain will come later, much less than Europe's.

completeness_estimate: 0.87 - first reader captured the curve, demand-forecast, shale, OPEC, storage, refining and LNG arguments; missed the fading-disruption detail, storage lag, Korean refinery exports, the oil-indexed gas pass-through, Asian contract-honouring and the closing humility remark; two minor over-fills (disruption size, cheap-crude reason).
